newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid hawk Malan said Reds, not blacks, were foe.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid hawk Malan said Reds, not blacks, were foe.

text.p: Magnus Malan said he was a Christian crusader against Bolshevism, but the hawkish apartheid defence minister ended up on trial for the slaughter of a family at prayer.
A South African court on Friday acquitted the defiant 66-year-old retired general of the murder almost a decade ago of 13 men, women and children at the home of a young black activist.
Prosecutors had said Malan's blessing for the creation of a covert military unit to fight black foes meant he was as steeped in the victims' blood as the men who pulled the triggers.
Malan, whose tough, stony mien seemed to suit a chief of a besieged apartheid regime that told its critics to go to hell, insists he never broke the law or gave orders to kill.
He admitted setting up paramilitary units to counter black opponents. But he said there was nothing sinister in it and killing children was unthinkable.
"The murder of 13 people goes absolutely against the grain of counter-revolutionary warfare," he told the court.
Communist revolution was the genuine fear of the one-time armed forces chief whom one colleague described as "a general who makes other military hawks sound like pet budgerigars".
"Our war is not against blacks," Malan said after a parade to show off white South Africa's military might, which he built up in the 1970s and 1980s and deployed in Angola and at home.
"Our war is against Reds. The enemy is international communism. The majority of our blacks are with us all the way."

But to many South African blacks, Malan is a figure of hate, a bogeyman they blame along with former police minister Adriaan Vlok for stoking the terror of township violence that raged right up until all-race elections in 1994 ended white rule.

Much of the blood flowed in fighting between supporters of Nelson Mandela's African National Congress and Zulu- traditionalist Inkatha rivals, whom Malan admits was given secret state military support.
A year before the poll Malan, an increasing liability from a dying era, left the reformist government led by F.W. de Klerk.
He had already been demoted to forestry minister because of close ties to the old guard of de Klerk's ousted predecessor, president P.W. Botha, and ANC demands that he must go.
Today he is bereft of powerful allies but is still close to right-wing leader General Constand Viljoen, who describes his friend as a strong-willed family man and a comedian.
Malan was born in January 1930 and joined the marines after graduating in military studies from Pretoria University.
He transferred to the army, studied military strategy in the United States and led the armed forces by the age of 46. He is married with three children.
